## Key findings

- **Inspection intervals** were set in 2019 and never revised, so the schedule no longer reflects the age of the fleet or the condition of its hulls.
- **Corrosion data** sits in three separate systems that do not share identifiers, so engineers reconcile it by hand before every quarterly review.
- **Coating records** are kept on paper at each site and are scanned only when an auditor asks for them.
- **Drone surveys** cover the upper decks well but miss the splash zone, where most of the wall loss is found.
- **Risk scores** are recalculated once a year by one analyst using a spreadsheet that has grown to forty tabs.
- **Repair backlogs** are tracked in the maintenance system, but the priority field is free text, so the backlog cannot be sorted by risk.
- **Training** for new inspectors is informal and depends on which senior inspector happens to be on shift.
- **Contractor reports** arrive as PDFs in four different templates, so findings cannot be compared without retyping them.
- **Budgets** are set before the risk scores are known, so money follows last year's plan rather than this year's risk.
- **Spare parts** for older pumps are held at one site only, and lead times for replacements have doubled since 2024.
- **Diving campaigns** are booked a year ahead, so a defect found in spring often waits until the following summer.
- **Thickness readings** are taken at fixed points that were chosen when the vessels were built, not where wall loss now occurs.
- **Cathodic protection** surveys are recorded in a separate tool that the integrity team cannot query directly.
- **Anomaly reports** are raised by email and copied into the register by hand, which loses the photographs attached to them.
- **Shutdown windows** are planned by operations without sight of the integrity backlog, so urgent repairs miss the window.
- **Handover notes** between shifts mention defects in free text that nobody searches later.
- **Third-party audits** find the same gaps every year because the actions they raise have no single owner.
- **Sensor data** from the corrosion probes is logged locally and overwritten after ninety days.
- **Material certificates** for repaired sections are filed by purchase order, not by location on the vessel.
- **Weld inspections** follow the original fabrication standard, which the class society has since revised twice.
- **Fatigue assessments** were last run in 2017 and assume a sea state that the vessels now exceed every winter.
- **Marine growth** is cleaned on a fixed cycle, which wastes diving time on clean hulls and leaves fouled ones too long.
- **Mooring chains** are inspected by a different contractor whose findings never reach the integrity register.
- **Deck penetrations** are not in any inspection plan, although two leaks last year started at one of them.
- **Firewater pipework** is inspected by the safety team using a scheme that does not match the integrity team's scheme.
- **Lessons learnt** from the 2025 incident were written up but never turned into changes to the inspection plan.
- **Key performance indicators** count inspections done, not defects closed, so the backlog grows while the indicators look healthy.
- **Software licences** for the corrosion model lapse every March and take weeks to renew.
- **Site visits** by the central team happen once a year, which is too rarely to see how the plan is carried out.
- **Decisions** on whether to repair or monitor a defect are not recorded, so the same defect is debated again at every review.
:::
